title: Tropical Cyclones
summary: How tropical cyclones form over warm oceans, why they spin, what the eye and eyewall are, why they are dangerous, and how scientists warn people.
poll: Scientists can do a lot to keep people safe from big storms.

versions.title: Big Storms at Sea
versions.text:
Some storms are huge. They spin like a top. They are called cyclones.

A cyclone starts at sea. The ocean must be warm. Some of the warm water goes up into the air. The wet air goes up and up. It makes big clouds. The warm sea gives the storm its power.

The air spins. The storm grows and grows.

The middle of the storm is the eye. The eye is calm. The sky there can be blue. But all around it is a ring of strong wind. It rains hard there.

The wind is fast. It can knock down trees. It brings lots of rain. The rain can flood towns. The storm can push the sea up onto the land, too.

Then the storm gets to land. It gets weak. It has no warm sea to feed it. Then it dies out.

In some lands, these storms have a new name. Some are called hurricanes.

People watch the storms from space. They warn towns. Then the people can get to a safe place.

versions.title: Big Storms at Sea
versions.text:
Some storms are so big that they can be seen from space. They spin like a giant top. They are called tropical cyclones.

A cyclone starts over the ocean. The water must be warm. Warm water turns into a gas in the air. The warm, wet air rises. It cools and makes big clouds. The warm sea gives the storm its power.

As the air rises, it starts to spin. The storm grows bigger and bigger. It can be hundreds of kilometers wide.

The middle of the storm is called the eye. The eye is calm. The sky there may even be blue. But all around the eye is a ring of very strong wind and rain.

A cyclone has very fast winds. They can knock down trees and homes. The storm also drops lots of rain. The rain can flood towns. The wind can push the sea up onto the land, too.

When a cyclone moves over land, it gets weak. It has no warm sea to feed it. Soon it dies out.

In some places, these storms have other names. Some are called hurricanes. Some are called typhoons.

People watch the storms from space. They warn towns. Then people can move to a safe place.

versions.title: Tropical Cyclones: Spinning Storms
versions.text:
Some storms are so big that you can see them from space. They spin like a big wheel. These storms are called tropical cyclones.

A tropical cyclone begins over a warm ocean. The sun heats the water. Some of the water turns into a gas. It goes up into the air. High up, the warm, wet air cools. Then it forms huge, dark clouds. The warm ocean gives the storm its power.

More air rushes in and goes up. Then the storm starts to spin. It can grow to be hundreds of kilometers wide.

The center of the storm is called the eye. The eye is calm. The sky there may even be clear. But around the eye is a thick ring of clouds with the strongest wind and rain.

A cyclone's winds can blow faster than a car on a highway. They can knock down trees. The storm also drops lots of rain. The rain can flood towns. Strong winds can even push the sea onto the land.

When a cyclone moves over land, it gets weaker. It has no warm sea water to feed it. So it slowly dies out.

In different parts of the world, these storms have different names. They may be called hurricanes, typhoons, or cyclones.

Scientists watch storms with satellites in space. They warn people early, so families can move to a safe place.

versions.title: Tropical Cyclones: Spinning Storms
versions.text:
Some storms are so big that people can see them from space. They spin like a giant wheel across the sea. These powerful storms are called tropical cyclones.

A tropical cyclone begins over a warm ocean near the equator. The sun heats the water. Some of it turns into a gas called water vapor. The warm, wet air rises high into the sky. There it cools and forms tall, dark clouds. The warm ocean is like fuel for the storm.

More air rushes in to take the place of the rising air. Then the whole storm begins to spin. A large cyclone can stretch hundreds of kilometers across.

The center of the storm is called the eye. Inside the eye, the air is calm. The sky may even be clear. But around the eye is a thick wall of clouds with the strongest winds and heaviest rain.

A cyclone's winds can blow faster than a car on a highway. They can tear roofs off buildings and knock down trees. The storm also dumps huge amounts of rain, which can flood towns. Strong winds can even push the sea onto the land.

When a cyclone moves over land, it begins to weaken. Without warm ocean water to feed it, the storm slowly dies out.

In different parts of the world, these storms have different names. Near America they are called hurricanes, and near Asia they are often called typhoons.

Scientists watch storms with satellites. They send out warnings, so families have time to move to a safe place.

versions.title: Tropical Cyclones: Storms That Spin
versions.text:
From space, a tropical cyclone looks like a giant white pinwheel turning slowly over the sea. Up close, it is one of the most powerful storms on Earth.

A tropical cyclone forms over warm ocean water near the equator. The water usually needs to be at least 26 degrees Celsius. The sun heats the sea, and some of the water evaporates. It turns into a gas called water vapor. The warm, moist air rises. High in the sky, it cools. Then the water vapor condenses into tiny drops that form tall clouds. As the vapor condenses, it gives off heat. This makes the air rise even faster. In this way, the warm ocean acts like fuel for the storm.

As air rushes in to replace the rising air, the turning of the Earth makes the whole storm spin. A large cyclone can stretch hundreds of kilometers across.

At the center is the eye, where the air is calm and the sky may be clear. Around the eye is the eyewall, a thick ring of clouds with the strongest winds and the heaviest rain.

A storm becomes a full tropical cyclone when its winds reach about 119 kilometers per hour. The winds can rip off roofs and knock down trees. Heavy rain can cause floods. The most dangerous part is often the storm surge, when the wind pushes the sea up onto the coast.

When a cyclone moves over land or cold water, it loses its fuel and weakens.

These storms are called hurricanes near America. Near East Asia they are called typhoons. The Arabian Sea has cyclones, too. In 2007, Cyclone Gonu struck Oman.

Scientists use satellites and computers to forecast where a storm will go. Their warnings give people time to reach safety.

versions.title: Tropical Cyclones: Storms That Spin
versions.text:
From space, a tropical cyclone looks like a giant white pinwheel turning slowly over the ocean. Up close, it is one of the most powerful and dangerous storms on Earth.

A tropical cyclone forms over warm ocean water near the equator, where the sea is usually at least 26 degrees Celsius. The sun heats the surface, and some of the water evaporates, becoming an invisible gas called water vapor. This warm, moist air rises fast. High in the sky, it cools. Then the water vapor condenses into tiny droplets that build towering clouds. When vapor condenses, it releases heat, which makes the air rise even faster. In this way, the warm ocean acts as fuel for the storm.

As more air rushes in to replace the rising air, the rotation of the Earth causes the whole system to spin. A large cyclone can stretch hundreds of kilometers across.

At the center is the eye, where the air is calm and the sky may even be clear. Surrounding the eye is the eyewall, a thick ring of clouds with the fiercest winds and the heaviest rain.

A storm officially becomes a tropical cyclone when its winds reach about 119 kilometers per hour. Such winds can rip off roofs and knock down trees. Heavy rain can cause serious floods. Often the most dangerous part is the storm surge, which happens when powerful winds push seawater up onto the coast.

When a cyclone moves over land or cooler water, it loses its fuel and gradually weakens.

These storms are called hurricanes near the Americas and typhoons near East Asia. The Arabian Sea also has cyclones. In 2007, Cyclone Gonu struck the coast of Oman.

Scientists use satellites and computers to forecast a storm's path. Their warnings give people time to reach safety.

versions.title: Tropical Cyclones: Engines of Wind and Water
versions.text:
Seen from space, a tropical cyclone resembles a gigantic white pinwheel rotating slowly over the ocean. Up close, it is one of the most powerful and destructive weather systems on Earth, capable of reshaping coastlines in a single day.

A tropical cyclone develops over warm ocean water near the equator, where the sea surface temperature is usually at least 26 degrees Celsius. The sun heats the water, and some of it evaporates into water vapor. This warm, moist air rises rapidly, and high in the atmosphere it cools, so the vapor condenses into droplets that build towering clouds. Because condensation releases heat, the surrounding air becomes warmer and rises even faster, which lowers the air pressure near the sea surface and draws in still more moist air. As long as warm water lies beneath it, this cycle allows the storm to intensify.

The rotation of the Earth deflects the inflowing air, so the entire system begins to spin. In the Northern Hemisphere, cyclones turn counterclockwise, while in the Southern Hemisphere they turn clockwise. A large cyclone can extend hundreds of kilometers across.

At the center lies the eye, a region of calm air and sometimes clear sky, surrounded by the eyewall, a dense ring of clouds containing the most violent winds and the heaviest rainfall.

A storm officially becomes a tropical cyclone when its sustained winds reach approximately 119 kilometers per hour. Such winds can tear off roofs, while torrential rain can cause severe flooding. Frequently the deadliest threat is the storm surge, which occurs when powerful winds drive seawater onto the coast.

When a cyclone travels over land or cooler water, it loses its supply of fuel and gradually weakens.

These storms are called hurricanes near the Americas and typhoons near East Asia. The Arabian Sea also experiences cyclones; in 2007, Cyclone Gonu struck the coast of Oman.

Each year, storms receive names from lists prepared in advance by an international weather organization, because short, distinctive names reduce confusion when several storms are active at the same time.

Meteorologists use satellites, aircraft, and computer models to forecast a storm's path, and their warnings give authorities time to evacuate people from threatened areas.

versions.title: Tropical Cyclones: Engines of Wind and Water
versions.text:
Seen from space, a tropical cyclone resembles a gigantic white pinwheel rotating slowly over the ocean. Up close, it is one of the most powerful and destructive weather systems on Earth, capable of reshaping entire coastlines within a single day.

A tropical cyclone develops over warm ocean water near the equator, where the sea surface temperature is usually at least 26 degrees Celsius. The sun heats the water, and some of it evaporates into water vapor. This warm, moist air rises rapidly, and high in the atmosphere it cools, so the vapor condenses into droplets that build towering clouds. Because condensation releases heat, the surrounding air becomes warmer and rises even faster, which lowers the air pressure near the sea surface and draws in additional moist air. As long as warm water lies beneath it, this self-reinforcing cycle allows the storm to intensify.

The rotation of the Earth deflects the inflowing air, so the entire system begins to spin; in the Northern Hemisphere, cyclones rotate counterclockwise, whereas in the Southern Hemisphere they rotate clockwise. A mature cyclone can extend hundreds of kilometers across.

At the center lies the eye, a region of calm air and sometimes clear sky, surrounded by the eyewall, a dense ring of clouds containing the most violent winds and the heaviest rainfall.

A storm officially becomes a tropical cyclone when its sustained winds reach approximately 119 kilometers per hour. Such winds can demolish roofs and uproot mature trees, while torrential rain, which may exceed a meter in some locations, can cause severe flooding far from the coast. Frequently the deadliest threat is the storm surge, which occurs when powerful winds drive seawater inland across low-lying coasts.

When a cyclone travels over land or cooler water, it loses its supply of fuel and gradually weakens.

These storms are called hurricanes near the Americas and typhoons near East Asia. The Arabian Sea also experiences cyclones; in 2007, Cyclone Gonu struck the coast of Oman.

Each year, storms receive names from alphabetical lists prepared in advance by an international weather organization, because short, distinctive names reduce confusion when several storms are active simultaneously in the same ocean.

Meteorologists use satellites, specially equipped aircraft, and computer models to forecast a storm's path and strength, and their warnings give authorities time to evacuate residents from threatened areas.

versions.title: Tropical Cyclones: Engines of Wind and Water
versions.text:
Viewed from space, a tropical cyclone resembles a gigantic white pinwheel rotating deliberately over the ocean. Up close, it is one of the most powerful and destructive atmospheric phenomena on Earth, capable of reshaping entire coastlines within a single day.

A tropical cyclone develops over warm ocean water near the equator, where the sea surface temperature generally exceeds 26 degrees Celsius. The sun heats the water, and some of it evaporates into water vapor. This warm, humid air ascends rapidly, and high in the atmosphere it cools, so the vapor condenses into droplets that construct towering clouds. Because condensation releases heat, the surrounding air becomes warmer and ascends even faster, which reduces the air pressure near the sea surface and draws in additional humid air. As long as warm water lies beneath it, this self-reinforcing cycle enables the storm to intensify.

The rotation of the Earth deflects the inflowing air, so the entire system begins to spin; in the Northern Hemisphere, cyclones rotate counterclockwise, whereas in the Southern Hemisphere they rotate clockwise. A mature cyclone can extend hundreds of kilometers across.

At the center lies the eye, a region of relatively calm air and occasionally clear sky, surrounded by the eyewall, a dense ring of clouds containing the most violent winds and the heaviest rainfall.

A storm officially becomes a tropical cyclone when its sustained winds reach approximately 119 kilometers per hour. Such winds can demolish buildings and uproot mature trees, while torrential precipitation, which occasionally exceeds a meter in particular locations, can cause catastrophic flooding far from the coastline. Frequently the deadliest threat is the storm surge, which occurs when powerful winds drive seawater inland across low-lying coastal communities.

When a cyclone travels over land or cooler water, it loses its supply of fuel and gradually weakens.

These storms are called hurricanes near the Americas and typhoons near East Asia. The Arabian Sea also experiences cyclones; in 2007, Cyclone Gonu struck the coast of Oman.

Each year, storms receive names from alphabetical lists prepared in advance by an international meteorological organization, because short, distinctive names substantially reduce confusion when several storms are active simultaneously in the same ocean basin. Scientists also classify the strongest Atlantic hurricanes into five categories according to their sustained wind speed, with Category 5 storms producing winds exceeding 250 kilometers per hour.

Meteorologists use satellites, specially equipped aircraft, and sophisticated computer models to forecast a storm's trajectory and intensity, and their warnings give authorities time to evacuate residents from threatened areas.

versions.title: Tropical Cyclones: Engines of Wind and Water
versions.text:
Viewed from space, a tropical cyclone resembles a gigantic white pinwheel rotating deliberately over the ocean, its spiraling bands of cloud stretching outward like the arms of a galaxy. Up close, it is one of the most powerful and destructive atmospheric phenomena on Earth, capable of reshaping entire coastlines within a single day.

A tropical cyclone develops over warm ocean water near the equator, where the sea surface temperature generally exceeds 26 degrees Celsius. Solar energy heats the water, and some of it evaporates into water vapor. This warm, humid air ascends rapidly, and high in the atmosphere it cools, so the vapor condenses into droplets that construct towering clouds. Because condensation releases considerable heat, the surrounding air becomes warmer and ascends even faster, which reduces the atmospheric pressure near the sea surface and draws in additional humid air. As long as warm water lies beneath it, this self-reinforcing cycle enables the storm to intensify dramatically.

The rotation of the Earth deflects the inflowing air, so the entire system begins to spin; in the Northern Hemisphere, cyclones rotate counterclockwise, whereas in the Southern Hemisphere they rotate clockwise. A mature cyclone can extend hundreds of kilometers across.

At the center lies the eye, a region of relatively calm air and occasionally clear sky, surrounded by the eyewall, a dense ring of clouds containing the most violent winds and the heaviest precipitation.

A storm officially becomes a tropical cyclone when its sustained winds reach approximately 119 kilometers per hour. Such winds can demolish buildings and uproot mature trees, while torrential precipitation, which occasionally exceeds a meter in particular locations, can produce catastrophic flooding considerably distant from the coastline. Frequently the deadliest threat is the storm surge, which occurs when powerful winds drive seawater inland across vulnerable, low-lying coastal communities.

When a cyclone travels over land or cooler water, it loses its supply of energy and gradually deteriorates.

These storms are designated hurricanes near the Americas and typhoons near East Asia. The Arabian Sea also experiences cyclones; in 2007, Cyclone Gonu struck the coast of Oman.

Each year, storms receive names from alphabetical lists prepared in advance by an international meteorological organization, because short, distinctive names substantially reduce confusion when several storms are active simultaneously in the same ocean basin. Scientists also classify the strongest Atlantic hurricanes into five categories according to their sustained wind speed, with Category 5 storms generating winds exceeding 250 kilometers per hour, which are capable of obliterating even sturdily constructed buildings.

Meteorologists utilize satellites, specially equipped reconnaissance aircraft, and sophisticated computer simulations to forecast a storm's trajectory and intensity, and their warnings give authorities sufficient time to evacuate residents from threatened areas.

MID.prompt: Explain, step by step, how warm ocean water becomes the fuel for a tropical cyclone. Use the words evaporate and condense.
checklist: I explained the steps in the right order.
I used evaporate and condense correctly.
I explained why warm water is needed.
MID.modelAnswer: First, the sun heats warm ocean water until some of it evaporates into water vapor. Then, as the moist air rises and cools, the water vapor begins to condense into towering clouds, and this releases heat that makes the air rise even faster. Warm water is needed because it provides the energy, or fuel, that keeps this whole cycle going and builds up the storm's powerful winds.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the article?
options: Cyclones are rare storms that seldom affect the lives of people near coasts.
Warm oceans drive a heat cycle that feeds cyclones, and forecasting reduces the danger.
Storm names are the most important tool for staying safe.
The Southern Hemisphere has stronger storms than the Northern Hemisphere.
questions.why: The article explains the self-reinforcing process that powers cyclones, their structure and hazards, and how meteorologists' warnings protect communities.

wrong.A: The article describes cyclones as powerful and destructive.
wrong.C: Naming reduces confusion, but it is one supporting detail.
wrong.D: The article only compares the direction of spin, not strength.

questions.stem: Which sequence correctly describes how a cyclone strengthens?
options: Air cools, sinks, and the pressure rises.
Rain falls, the sea cools, and winds increase.
The storm reaches land, then gains moisture from the soil, then spins faster.
Water evaporates, vapor condenses and gives off heat, and air rises faster.
questions.why: The article describes evaporation, condensation releasing heat, faster rising air, lower pressure, and more moist air being drawn in.

wrong.A: Sinking air and rising pressure are the opposite of what the article describes.
wrong.B: A cooling sea would weaken the storm.

questions.stem: According to the article, what happens to the air pressure near the sea surface when the warmed air rises faster?
options: It drops, which draws in more moist air.
It rises, which pushes the clouds away.
It stays the same, because the ocean controls it.
It drops, which makes the rain stop.
questions.why: The article states that the faster-rising air lowers the air pressure near the sea surface and draws in additional moist air.

wrong.B: The article says the pressure is reduced, not raised.
wrong.C: The article says the pressure changes.
wrong.D: The pressure does drop, but it draws in moist air and feeds the storm rather than stopping rain.

questions.stem: A cyclone forms south of the equator. In which direction will it most likely rotate?
options: Counterclockwise
It will not rotate at all
Clockwise
It will change direction every hour
questions.why: The article states that cyclones rotate counterclockwise in the Northern Hemisphere but clockwise in the Southern Hemisphere.

wrong.A: Counterclockwise rotation is typical of the Northern Hemisphere.
wrong.B: The Earth's rotation causes all cyclones to spin.
wrong.D: The article does not say storms change direction like this.

questions.stem: In the article, the cycle "allows the storm to intensify." Which word could replace intensify?
options: Disappear

Slow down
Move away
questions.why: The cycle of rising warm air feeds the storm, so it becomes stronger.

wrong.A: The storm disappears only after losing its fuel.
wrong.C: The cycle speeds the storm up rather than slowing it.
wrong.D: Intensify is about strength, not movement.

questions.stem: Why do weather organizations give storms short names, according to the article?
options: To show which country caused the storm

To reduce confusion when several storms are active

questions.stem: What can you infer about why warnings are issued days before a cyclone reaches the coast?

wrong.B: The article says people are moved away from threatened areas.
wrong.C: Forecasts give a likely path; they are not exact.
wrong.D: Cyclones are dangerous over the sea, too, though the article focuses on coasts.

questions.stem: Why does the author begin by describing how a cyclone looks from space?
options: To explain how satellites are launched

HIGH.prompt: Explain why a tropical cyclone can keep growing over warm water but weakens over land. Use evidence about heat, rising air, and pressure.
checklist: I explained the self-reinforcing cycle over warm water.
I explained why the storm weakens over land.
I used precise vocabulary and evidence from the article.
HIGH.modelAnswer: A tropical cyclone can keep growing over warm water because rising warm air releases heat as water vapor condenses, which lowers the pressure and makes the air rise even faster, pulling in more moist air to intensify the storm in a self-reinforcing cycle, while the rotation of the Earth makes the whole system spin. This cycle depends entirely on warm ocean water as fuel, so once the cyclone moves over land or cooler water, that fuel source disappears and the storm gradually weakens. Meteorologists track this pattern with satellites, and their forecasts give coastal communities time to evacuate before the storm's strongest winds and heaviest rain arrive.
